units.translation: ⟦1⟧ 63. 449. ⟦2⟧ can be understood as at 99 'I am accused', see V. 199, but also 'I have the guilt'. Then Apollo turns to Athena, who according to Attic usage is ⟦3⟧ of the trial (Meier-Schömann-Lipsius 45, 13); this procedure (present tense) may now go forward, and finally, according to the wisdom of the goddess (⟦4⟧ 667, ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧; ⟦7⟧ 'however'), the trial may be brought to an end and decided (aorist ⟦8⟧ by the judges). On ⟦9⟧ see on 86. Thereupon Athena gives the Erinyes the floor and sets up the general (though self-evident) principle, in words strongly reminiscent of the opening formula of later Attic court speeches, Lysias 12, 3 ⟦10⟧. 585–608. The Erinyes correspond to the (later and certainly also customary in Aeschylus' time) form of an accusation only in the one respect that they too promise brevity; of ⟦11⟧, however, nothing is to be noticed, nor of a connected exposition, since in place of the entire accusation speech comes the questioning of the accused. Such questioning also occurs in later court speeches, only not as the main thing or replacing the accusation (so Lysias 12, 25); since Orestes now not only answers with yes and no but defends himself, the whole hearing for and against is already given in essence. When afterwards Apollo appears as defender, the Erinyes in between also make their arguments, and likewise at greater length; thus there are two hearings, only to be compared with accusation and defense insofar as in the first the accusation has the first word, in the second the defense. So as in Aristophanic dispute scenes: in the Clouds first the ⟦12⟧ presents his case, with objections from the ⟦13⟧, and then the latter with corresponding participation of the opponent, and in the Frogs Aeschylus and Euripides likewise. Since the promised brevity in V. 585 is contrasted with the great number of the Erinyes, Weil has rightly inferred that the individual ones speak one after another: the first with two verses, then ten with one each, then the last with two. Thus the number twelve of the chorus results here, as in Agamemnon 1348 ff., unless one assumes there, which seems to me fundamentally wrong, that the three choreuts who previously heard the cries of woe from the palace and initiated the deliberation are thereby dispensed from expressing their opinion. For the Erinyes everything actually reduces to the question of fact, yet they also go somewhat into the motives, according to Athena's instruction at 426.
